data.text/markdown:
Bayesian regression: same model, a new way to express uncertainty

An interactive companion to A Better Way to Learn Bayesian Statistics

Start here: drag a point in the first experiment. Then change your prior and watch what happens to the same regression slope. No coin flips required. Based on Simplistics (QuantPsych)'s video. The video introduces a course philosophy, not a worked numerical analysis. Its backbone is our backbone: familiar linear models → familiar visualizations → new Bayesian interpretations. The experiments below are an original Python companion. You need: basic regression intuition. Allow: about 20–30 minutes.
  1. Move data and fit a familiar line.
  2. Add a prior and see a posterior.
  3. Interpret credible intervals and predictions.
  4. Check fit, explore real data, and test your intuition.
Color key: gray = classical/data-only; blue = prior; orange = posterior; purple = uncertainty for a new observation.
Model contract. We use a normal linear model with a user-specified, known residual standard deviation σ. This allows exact Bayesian answers and instant interaction. Ordinary lm() / brm() also estimate σ; their intervals need not match ours. Our posterior draws are independent normal draws, not MCMC.

1 · Keep the regression you already know

Video connection: incremental learning (5:55) and the Avengers example (8:23, 11:01). The video's example predicts PTSD from agility. Here we use fictional teaching data, not clinical measurements or the video's original dataset. No causal claim is implied. ||[ \mathrm{PTSD}_i = \alpha + \beta x_i + \epsilon_i, \qquad x_i=(\mathrm{agility}_i-50)/10, \qquad \epsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma^2). ||]So α is the expected score at agility 50; β is the change in expected score for 10 more agility points. The model stays the same when we change the estimation framework. Try this: (1) drag one point upward; (2) compare 12 with 60 observations; (3) choose “Curved” and ask whether a straight line is adequate. An OLS line minimizes squared vertical errors—it does not prove the model is appropriate.

2 · Same slope, now with a prior

Video connection: changing frameworks and adding prior syntax (11:01–14:00). A prior expresses plausible coefficient values before these observations. The likelihood scores how well coefficients explain the observations under the model. The posterior combines both: ||[ p(\alpha,\beta\mid y,X,\sigma)\ \propto\ p(y\mid X,\alpha,\beta,\sigma)\,p(\alpha)\,p(\beta). ||]Here ||(\alpha\sim\mathcal N(50,30^2)||) and ||(\beta\sim\mathcal N(m,s^2)||), independently. Change m (where the prior is centered) and s (how strongly it concentrates). Smaller s means a stronger prior. σ is residual scatter around a line, not uncertainty about its slope. Predict first: if the data suggest a negative slope but the prior insists on +6, where will the posterior go? Try this: (1) set m = +6 and s = 0.5; (2) widen s to 15; (3) switch from 12 to 60 observations above. A strong prior matters most when data are weak. Priors should have a defensible origin; tuning them until an answer is attractive is not validation.

3 · A posterior is a collection of plausible lines

A coefficient table can hide the central idea: we have uncertainty about α and β, so many lines remain plausible. Each orange line below is one joint draw from the posterior. The faint lines show other draws. These are possible parameter values, not fresh datasets. A 95% credible interval contains 95% of posterior probability for the specified quantity, conditional on the data, prior, and model. A 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed true parameter in 95% of repeated datasets under its assumptions; that coverage is not a posterior probability statement about this particular interval. Try this: (1) press Play and watch plausible lines; (2) move the probe toward an edge; (3) increase prior strength above and watch the fan narrow. A narrower answer can reflect a stronger assumption, not more evidence.

4 · Predicting an average is easier than predicting a person

Move the probe agility in the widget above. The orange interval below expresses uncertainty about the population mean at that agility. The purple interval predicts one new observation, so it also includes residual variation: ||[ \operatorname{Var}(y_{new}\mid x_{new},D) =\operatorname{Var}(\alpha+\beta x_{new}\mid D)+\sigma^2. ||]Try this: (1) probe agility 50, then 90; (2) increase σ; (3) use the 60-observation preset. More data can locate the mean accurately without making individual outcomes predictable. All intervals are conditional on this model.

data.text/html:
At agility 50: expected score 41.4

95% mean credible interval: [37.1, 45.6]
95% posterior predictive interval: [26.1, 56.7]
Selected draw slope: +0.88. The orange dot in the widget shows one plausible mean, not a random person's outcome.The Gaussian teaching model can predict scores outside 0–100. That is a model limitation to check, especially near boundaries; Bayesian inference does not fix a mismatched likelihood.

data.text/markdown:
5 · A posterior can be precise and still fit badly

Video connection: visualize fit/misfit, compare fits, and evaluate prior choices. The video's repeated workflow is estimate → visualize → compare. Start by asking whether your model can generate data resembling what you observe. Below, residuals are observed scores minus the posterior mean line. We also simulate 1,000 replicated datasets from the posterior predictive distribution, at the same agilities, and compare their residual RMS with the observed one. Try this: select Curved in section 1. Can you see structure in the residuals? Then increase σ: a larger noise assumption can hide the RMS mismatch without removing the curve. A single diagnostic cannot certify a model.

6 · What changes when software uses MCMC?

Video connection: output, chains, warm-up, and R-hat (about 12:20–14:00). We solved a special model exactly. More general models often need Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to approximate the posterior. MCMC produces dependent draws; more iterations are not more observations.
Term Practical interpretation
Chain One run of the sampler, usually with its own starting point
Warm-up Initial iterations used to adapt the algorithm and settle; excluded from reported posterior summaries
R-hat Compares within- and between-chain variation; modern rank-normalized split R-hat near 1 is reassuring, not proof
Effective sample size (ESS) How much information dependent draws contain relative to independent draws; inspect bulk and tail ESS
Divergences For Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, warning signs that parts of the posterior may not be explored correctly
In practice, investigate R-hat above roughly 1.01, low ESS, divergences, and poor trace plots. Good sampler diagnostics establish neither good model fit nor good priors.

A visual preview—not an MCMC implementation

Switch among these illustrative traces. “Sticky” follows a stationary AR(1) process; “Separated” deliberately offsets chains. We do not report an imitation R-hat.

data.text/markdown:
7 · Sandbox: take the same workflow to real observations

Now use R's classic cars dataset: 50 measurements of speed (mph) and stopping distance (feet), recorded in the 1920s. These are historical observations, not modern braking guidance. The values are embedded below so this experiment works offline. Dataset documentation · CSV mirror · Source: Ezekiel (1930), Methods of Correlation Analysis. We model ||(\mathrm{distance}=\alpha+\beta(\mathrm{speed}-15)+\epsilon||). Now β is feet per additional mph, and α is mean stopping distance at 15 mph. We use ||(\alpha\sim\mathcal N(40,40^2)||) and your slope prior below; σ is again assumed known. Challenges:
  1. Make a negative prior conflict with the upward data trend. How strong must it be to matter?
  2. Compare 10 with 50 observations, keeping the prior and σ fixed.
  3. Predict at 25 mph, then at 35 mph. A model's tidy extrapolation is not new evidence.
  4. Inspect the residual plot. Would constant noise and a straight line deserve closer checking?
The subset order is fixed and randomized, so increasing n retains earlier observations.

8 · Check your intuition

Make your predictions, then reveal feedback. The numerical question is tied to your current Avengers experiment: what is the posterior probability that its slope is negative? Try reasoning from the slope-density plot before looking back at its readout.

5/5

  • ✅ Interval: A credible interval is a posterior statement about the parameter, conditional on assumptions.
  • ✅ Prior: Information, not a magic sample size, determines the relative influence of likelihood and prior.
  • ✅ Prediction: Predictive variance adds σ² to uncertainty about the mean.
  • ✅ Mcmc: Computation can improve approximation; it cannot create new observations or fix a wrong likelihood.
  • ✅ Probability: 25.2%. Your guess is 2.2 percentage points away (within 5 earns the point).
Change the experiments and try again. Understanding the explanation matters more than the score.

Your new mental model

Familiar idea Bayesian addition Remember
Regression line Distribution over possible lines Same α, β, predictors, and response
Coefficient estimate Posterior mean, interval, and directional probability Interpret conditional on prior, likelihood, and observed data
Modeling assumptions Explicit priors as well as a likelihood Strong assumptions can make a wrong answer precise
Prediction Posterior predictive distribution Include parameter uncertainty and residual variation
Residual checks Posterior predictive checks Good computation does not guarantee a good model
More complicated models Different likelihoods, links, or group effects Keep the estimate → visualize → compare workflow

Connecting this back to the video's R syntax

# Schematic examples; use your own avengers data frame.
classical <- lm(PTSD ~ agility, data = avengers)
bayesian <- brms::brm(
  PTSD ~ agility, data = avengers,
  prior = brms::prior(normal(0, 1), class = "b", coef = "agility")
)
The R slope above is per one agility point. Our teaching slope is per ten: divide our slope prior mean and SD by 10 when translating to that raw predictor. The example R prior is illustrative, not a recommendation. brm() also estimates residual σ and has other priors; it is not the identical model used here. The video describes consistent flexplot functions such as estimates, visualize, compare.fits, and model.comparison, and says its Bayesian integration was not published at recording time. We follow that workflow without assuming those integrations are available in your installed R packages.

Where to go next

  1. Estimate σ rather than treating it as known, using a general Bayesian modeling package.
  2. Check prior predictive simulations before fitting real data.
  3. Compare predictive performance using held-out data or suitable cross-validation; visual similarity alone is not model selection. We did not compute Bayes factors here.
  4. Add a predictor, a group-level effect, or a likelihood/link for a binary or count response.
  5. When using MCMC, inspect convergence, ESS, and sampler warnings before interpreting results.
